Solitary pulmonary nodule

  • Definition: single, spherical, well-circumscribed, radiologic opacity ≤ 3cm and surrounded completely by normal lung. Patient completely asymptomatic.
  • 0.2% incidentaloma finding on all CXR and CT-chest
  • The most common presentation of lung cancer → asymptomatic (incidental). 438
Notes

Solitary Pulmonary Nodule (SPN)

DEFINITION
A single, spherical, well-circumscribed radiologic opacity ≤3 cm, completely surrounded by normal lung, found incidentally in an asymptomatic patient on CXR or CT.
≤3 cm = nodule | >3 cm = mass.
  • The cut-off to call a lung lesion a nodule → 3 cm or less. 439

Differential diagnosis

Notes

Differential Diagnosis — Think in Categories

Vascular, infectious, traumatic, autoimmune, malformation, inflammatory, neoplastic. Whenever you land on neoplasia, walk the branch all the way down:

SOLITARY PULMONARY NODULE → NEOPLASTIC BRANCH
Benign Hamartoma, granuloma and other non- malignant lesions.·Malignant — Primary Originates from the lung itself.·Malignant — Secondary Metastasis from another organ, e.g. colon cancer → lung.
  • Malignant lung lesion → carcinoid tumour (a low-grade malignant neuroendocrine tumour; hamartoma, granular cell tumour and sclerosing haemangioma are benign). 429 ×3
  • N (neoplasia):
  • Benign: hamartoma, lipoma, fibroma, neurofibroma, leiomyoma, angioma
  • Malignant:
  • Primary: Adeno, scc, large cell, small cell, carcinoid, extra nodal lymphoma
  • Metastatic: breast, colon, melanoma (these three are the most common lung mets), H&N, renal, sarcoma, germ cell tumor. Most common endobronchial mets: colon, breast, renal
  • Miscellaneous: plasmacytoma, schwannoma
  • Others: amyloidoma, rounded atelectasis, intrapulmonary lymph node, pseudotumor ( located fluid), mucoid impaction)
  • Independent predictor factor of malignancy:
  • older age
  • current or previous smoker
  • history of extra-thoracic cancer
  • Diameter
  • spiculated
  • Location in the upper lobes.
Notes

Predictors of Malignancy

Older age
Current or previous smoking
Previous extrathoracic cancer → possible lung metastasis
Previous intrathoracic cancer → possible recurrence
Increasing nodule diameter → higher probability
Spiculated margins
Upper-lobe location — attributed to tracheobronchial architecture and carcinogen deposition
CAVEAT
Upper-lobe predominance is a probability, not a rule — lung cancer still occurs in the lower lobes.

Lung cancer screening

  • What is screening?
  • WHO definition: Screening is defined as the presumptive identification of unrecognized disease in an apparently healthy, asymptomatic population by means of tests, examinations or other procedures that can be applied rapidly and easily to the target population
  • What are the benefits of screening?
  • Early diagnosis
Notes

Screening vs Surveillance vs Diagnosis

TermWhat it isDefining feature
ScreeningTesting an asymptomatic target population for disease that may not be presentNo symptoms + belongs to a risk/target population + no previously known abnormality being followed
SurveillanceFollow-up of a known abnormalitye.g. treated cancer, premalignant lesion — the abnormality already exists
DiagnosisInvestigation prompted by symptoms or signsThe patient presents with a complaint
FORMAL DEFINITION OF SCREENING
The presumptive identification of unrecognized disease in an apparently healthy, asymptomatic population, using tests, examinations or procedures that can be applied rapidly and easily and that should not harm the patient. It requires a defined target population.
  • Which diseases are suitable for screening?

1. significant negative impact on health

2. an identifiable asymptomatic period

3. improved outcomes with early intervention

4. Risk factors

  • What is the best screening modality?

6. be capable of detecting a high proportion of disease in its preclinical state

7. be safe to administer

8. be reasonable in cost

9. lead to demonstrated improved health outcomes

10. be widely available, as must the interventions that follow a positive result

5.

Notes

What Makes a Disease and a Test Suitable for Screening

The disease should…The test should…
Have a significant negative health impactDetect a high proportion of disease
Have an identifiable asymptomatic periodBe safe
Have improved outcomes with early interventionBe of reasonable cost
Have identifiable risk factors that allow a target population to be definedShow demonstrated improvement in health outcomes and be widely available
Notes

Lung Cancer Screening

Why lung cancer qualifiesRisks of screening
Curable when detected very early — Stage I survival quoted up to ~90%, versus ≤30% for stages III–IVOverdiagnosis of indolent tumors that would never have affected lifespan
Has an asymptomatic periodPatient anxiety
Symptoms, when they come, are nonspecific (cough, shortness of breath)Complications of downstream procedures — CT-guided biopsy → hemorrhage, pneumothorax
Major health burden, driven by smoking prevalenceFalse positives and false negatives
Has identifiable risk factors and an available screening modalityRadiation exposure and incidental findings
THE RISK–BENEFIT PRINCIPLE
In the target population, the benefits of screening outweigh the risks. In a non-target population, the risks may outweigh the benefits. This single idea is why eligibility criteria exist at all.

Why?

  • Curable at early staging ( survival: stage1 80% vs stage 3 30%)
  • Asymptomatic in early stages, symptoms are nonspecific
  • Major health hazard
  • Has risk factors
  • Available modalities

Benefits vs Risks

Lung cancer screening guidelines

Notes

NCCN Guidance and the Evidence Base

NCCN produces frequently updated cancer guidelines based primarily on high-level evidence; where strong evidence is lacking, recommendations may incorporate expert-panel opinion.
Earlier screening studies using chest X-ray failed to show sufficient benefit — small early lung cancers may simply not be visible on CXR.
CT screening was historically held back by concerns about cost and radiation exposure.
Landmark evidenceModalityResult
NLST (North American)Low-dose CT (LDCT)~20% reduction in lung-cancer mortality
Subsequent major European trialLow-dose CT (LDCT)~30% reduction in lung-cancer mortality
HIGH-RISK POPULATION — WHO GETS SCREENED
Age ≥50 years
≥20 pack-year smoking history
Qualifying patient with no abnormality detected → annual low-dose CT
Abnormality detected → leave the annual-screening pathway and follow the appropriate nodule/screening algorithm
COUNSELING EXTRAS
Not part of the core criteria, but useful when a qualifying patient is hesitant: family history of lung cancer, previous relevant exposures, and COPD. Counseling is integral because screening investigates a disease the patient may not actually have.
  • Asymptomatic 52-year-old, 30 pack-years, quit 10 years ago → annual low-dose CT. 442

Lung Cancer

Types

  • Non-small cell lung cancer
  • Adenocarcinoma
  • Squamous cell carcinoma
  • Adenosquamous cell carcinoma
  • Large cell carcinoma
  • Carcinoid tumors: typical and atypical
  • Small Cell lung cancer
  • Lung cancer treated non-surgically → small cell carcinoma (chemo-radiotherapy). 438 ×2
Notes

Lung Cancer: General Features & Histology

THE CORE CLINICAL PROBLEM
An aggressive malignancy with high mortality that frequently produces no specific symptoms until the disease is advanced — approximately 80% of patients were described as asymptomatic. When symptoms do appear (cough, hemoptysis, recurrent respiratory infections) they are nonspecific and occur without cancer too. This is precisely the argument for screening.
Notes

Histologic Types

Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC)
Adenocarcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma
Large-cell carcinoma
Small-Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)
Most aggressive type discussed
Most present at an advanced stage
Usually considered non-resectable

Pulmonary Neuroendocrine Tumors — One Cell of Origin, Very Different Behavior

Spectrum (best → worst prognosis)Key point
Typical carcinoidBest prognosis of the spectrum
Atypical carcinoidIntermediate behavior
Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinomaAggressive
Small-cell lung cancerWorst prognosis of the spectrum
All share a neuroendocrine cell origin but differ substantially in biological behavior.
EXCEPTION WORTH REMEMBERING
"Non-resectable" for SCLC is a generalization, not an absolute. Very early incidentally detected disease — e.g. a 2 cm localized SCLC — may be resectable. Untreated advanced SCLC can progress extremely rapidly, with survival quoted at approximately 6 months.

Presentation

  • symptomatic vs asymptomatic ( screening )
  • Asymptomatic 80%
  • Cough, hemoptysis, recurrent respiratory infections, dyspnea, and chest pain

Notes

Lung Cancer Workup

History & physical → basic labs → CXR → contrast CT chest → tissue diagnosis → staging → mediastinal assessment when indicated → pulmonary function / operability assessment → treatment
StepWhat to cover
HistoryPresenting symptoms and risk factors. A detailed smoking history: when started, when/if stopped, duration since cessation, packs per day, and type of smoking.
Also reviewAllergies, medications — and in a surgical candidate, particularly anticoagulants and steroid use.
Physical examInspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation. Frequently normal in asymptomatic patients unless substantial disease is present.
CXROften the initial imaging that demonstrates the abnormality.
CT chestObtain with IV contrast — contrast distinguishes masses from blood vessels and other thoracic structures.
VAPING COUNTS
Vaping, IQOS and shisha are smoking. Switching to them is not smoking cessation, and the smoking history must be recorded accordingly.
  • Screening candidate → 51-year-old with 30 pack-years (not < 20 pack-years, not < 50 years old). 441

Investigations

  • To determine operability ( patient ) and resectability (cancer)
  • CXR
  • CT chest (infused)
  • Tissue Biopsy
  • PET- CT scan, MRI brain with contrast(Stage II, IIIA) (Stage IB [optional]
  • CT abdomen, bone scan ( if PET-CT scan not available, or more information is needed)
  • Bronchoscopy Mediastonoscopy/ EBUS ( T2 ((T1 MLN mets 5-7%)) , central, enraged LN or PET avid N1 or N2 )
  • Pulmonary Function Tests
  • Most accurate statement on NSCLC staging → mediastinoscopy/mediastinotomy stages NSCLC with > 90% accuracy (fixed — the recall keyed "VATS is used routinely", which is not true; CT chest is always needed, MRI is not superior). 436
Notes

Tissue Diagnosis

NON-NEGOTIABLE RULE
A cancer diagnosis requires tissue confirmation. Do not give chemotherapy or radiotherapy on the basis of imaging or clinical suspicion alone. Diagnosis must precede staging procedures.

Chest x-ray

Ct lungs

Biopsy

Notes

Biopsy Route Follows Tumor Location

LocationApproachWhy
Peripheral lesionCT-guided percutaneous biopsy — needle placement visualized on CT, usually performed by interventional radiologyThe lesion sits close to the chest wall, so the needle path is short and safe
Central lesionAirway-based sampling via bronchoscopyA long percutaneous needle passage toward the hilum may be unsafe
Bronchoscopy
A flexible scope/camera passed through the airway to directly inspect the trachea and bronchi, used for both visualization and biopsy. Particularly useful when the lesion is central or endobronchial.
WHY BRONCHOSCOPY IS DONE ROUTINELY BEFORE LUNG RESECTION
1. To detect a synchronous endobronchial tumor that may be too small to appreciate on CT.
2. To confirm bronchial anatomy and identify anatomical variants / aberrant bronchi before resection.

Ct-guided biopsy

PET scan

Notes

PET/CT

Role: primarily staging — lymph-node involvement and distant metastases.

PRINCIPLE
Radioisotope-labeled glucose is administered. Hypermetabolic cells consume more glucose → greater isotope accumulation → increased PET uptake.
UPTAKE ≠ CANCER
Increased PET uptake also occurs with infection and inflammation. Suspicious uptake may therefore still require tissue confirmation.
SituationWhat to know
Physiologic uptakeBrain is normally highly metabolically active; kidneys and bladder light up because the tracer is renally excreted.
Suspected brain metastasisPET is unreliable for the brain (normal brain is hypermetabolic). Best test = MRI brain. If MRI cannot be done → contrast-enhanced CT brain.
PET unavailableComplete the metastatic workup with what you have: already-obtained CT chest + CT abdomen/pelvis + bone scan + brain MRI when indicated.

CT Abdomen & Pelvis

Bone Scan

Brain MRI

  • Lung-cancer patient with headache, suspected metastasis → brain MRI. 439 ×2

Transbronchial FNA

EBUS

Trans-esophageal FNA

Mediastinoscopy

Notes

Methods of Mediastinal Assessment

MethodHow it worksReach / yield
EBUS endobronchial ultrasoundBronchoscope containing an ultrasound component; needle/FNA sampling performed under ultrasound guidance, not direct visual inspection. Generally done by a pulmonologist and requires specific training.Peritracheal nodes, peribronchial nodes and other accessible masses — structures not visible through ordinary bronchoscopy. Less invasive.
Bronchoscopic FNAFNA passed through a conventional bronchoscope; sampling directed by anatomical knowledge.Limited by what can be seen directly. Example: station 7 nodes lie beneath the carina. EBUS improves accuracy with real- time ultrasound.
EUS endoscopic ultrasound via esophagusThe esophagus lies close to many mediastinal structures, giving an alternative sampling window.Peri-esophageal lymph nodes and other lesions accessible from the esophagus — lung cancer does metastasize there.
MediastinoscopySurgical staging: small suprasternal incision → mediastinoscope passed along the trachea → nodes biopsied directly.Higher tissue yield — large chunks, occasionally essentially the whole node. More tissue than needle FNA.
EBUS BALLOON — WHY IT EXISTS
Ultrasound needs a transmitting medium, and gel cannot practically be placed inside the airway. EBUS therefore uses a balloon containing aqueous solution to provide ultrasound coupling.
CHOOSING BETWEEN THEM & GETTING THE SEQUENCE RIGHT
EBUS = less invasive; mediastinoscopy = higher tissue yield. The choice depends on the clinical situation and how much tissue is needed. Both are principally staging procedures: first establish the diagnosis with an appropriate biopsy, then stage — including invasive nodal staging when indicated. Older chest-wall mediastinoscopic approaches are largely obsolete; thoracic lesions can now often be accessed by VATS.
COMPLICATIONS OF MEDIASTINOSCOPY
Major vascular injury — e.g. azygos-vein injury — potentially catastrophic and may require sternotomy.
Esophageal injury → mediastinitis.
Pneumothorax — chest tube if clinically necessary.
Should be performed by experienced operators.

Staging

Notes

Mediastinal Lymph-Node Staging

Nodal disease progresses N1 → N2 → N3, with progressively worse prognosis — and, critically, the N stage is what decides whether surgery is the first step.

StageAnatomyManagement implication
N1Ipsilateral hilar / intrapulmonary nodes — same side as the primary tumorN0 and N1 generally proceed initially to resection. N0 → usually no postoperative chemo; N1 → postoperative (adjuvant) chemotherapy
N2Ipsilateral mediastinal nodesChanges initial management — may be nonoperative initially, or treated with neoadjuvant therapy → reassessment → resection in selected patients
N3Contralateral mediastinal / hilar involvementMore advanced disease — usually not operable or resectable
THE PRINCIPLE TO CARRY INTO THE EXAM
N1 usually does not change the initial surgical step; N2 and N3 may change treatment from the outset. This is exactly why large, central or otherwise high-risk tumors require invasive mediastinal nodal assessment before definitive treatment is chosen.
Notes

TNM Staging & Stage-Directed Treatment

T = primary tumor | N = lymph nodes | M = distant metastasis → together they determine stage I–IV, which directly drives prognosis and treatment.
StageSimplified concept from the lectureTreatment
Stage ISmall, localized tumor; no nodal or distant metastasisSurgery alone most of the time
Stage IIGenerally larger / local disease; simplified as no distant metastasisMultimodality: surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, radiation, targeted therapy,
Stage IIIGenerally significant regional nodal involvement / locally advanced diseaseimmunotherapy — exact combination depends on tumor characteristics and staging
Stage IIIB and aboveBeyond the resectable window in the simplified approachGenerally not surgically resectable → chemotherapy/systemic treatment, radiation therapy, palliation when appropriate
Stage IVDistant metastasisSystemic and palliative management
SIMPLIFICATION WARNING
The stage I–IV descriptions above are a deliberate simplification — some stage II tumors can have nodal involvement. Use TNM itself for the real assignment.

TREATMENT

  • Based on the staging
  • Stage1 : surgery only ( small tumor with no LN or distant mets)
  • Stage II and IIIA: surgery with adjuvant or neoadjuvant treatment ( chemotherapy and radiation therapy)
  • Stage IIIB and above: chemotherapy and radiation therapy , palliation
Notes

Resectability vs Operability

ResectabilityOperability
The questionCan the tumor be removed surgically with therapeutic intent?Can this patient physiologically tolerate the planned operation?
Determined byCancer stage / anatomical extentGeneral functional and medical condition; pulmonary reserve
Key considerationDistant metastasis = stage IV — cells are already systemic, so surgery usually has no curative role. Earlier stages are more likely resectable.Will the remaining lung after resection provide adequate function?
Assessed withImaging, PET/CT, invasive nodal stagingPulmonary function tests (PFTs) — specific measurements and calculations determine whether the patient can tolerate the proposed amount of lung resection
ONE-LINE VERSION
Resectability = tumor / stage. Operability = patient / function. Curative surgery requires both.

Surgical Treatment

  • Preoperative assessment :
  • General health status.
  • Lung function ( PFTs, VO2 max, ABG, V-Q scan)
  • Anatomical resection ( take vein, artery, and bronchus with lymph nodes) :
  • Segmentectomy
  • Lobectomy
  • Pneumonectomy

Not wedge resection ( non-anatomical resection)

Notes

Surgical Resection of Lung Cancer

PRINCIPLE OF CANCER SURGERY
Malignant tumors should generally undergo anatomical resection — removing the anatomical unit together with its arterial supply, venous drainage, bronchus and associated lymph nodes. The purpose is to maximize the probability of complete oncologic resection.
ResectionTypeWhat is removed / when used
SegmentectomyAnatomicalA bronchopulmonary segment with its associated bronchovascular structures
LobectomyAnatomicalAn entire lobe — the most commonly used lung-cancer anatomical resection. Right lung = 3 lobes, left lung = 2 lobes; each lobe subdivides into segments
PneumonectomyAnatomicalThe entire lung — not performed simply because cancer is present
Wedge resectionNon- anatomicalA wedge-shaped portion of lung without formal dissection of segmental bronchovascular anatomy. Used for diagnostic purposes, benign lesions, and pulmonary metastases — e.g. colon cancer metastatic to lung may be treated with a limited wedge rather than an anatomical resection
RULE OF THUMB
Use the least amount of lung resection that achieves adequate oncologic treatment, escalating only when necessary. Preservation of functioning lung matters.
  • Early NSCLC of the right lower lobe (T1N0M0) → right lower lobectomy. 437 ×7

Thoracotomy

Notes

Surgical Approaches

Open abdomen = laparotomy ↔ open chest = thoracotomy | Minimally invasive abdomen = laparoscopy/robotic ↔ minimally invasive chest = VATS or robotic-assisted (RATS)
Notes

Thoracotomy

A large open thoracic incision. Avoid when possible, but it may be required for very large tumors, significant intraoperative bleeding, or any situation where conversion improves patient safety or allows complete cancer resection.

SURGICAL PRIORITIES — IN ORDER
1. Complete cancer resection.
2. Patient safety and survival through the operation.
Conversion to thoracotomy is appropriate whenever it is needed to achieve these goals.
THE PAIN CASCADE
Thoracotomy is a very painful incision — described as potentially more painful than sternotomy because of intercostal injury. Pain → poor respiratory effort → postoperative pneumonia, which matters enormously after lung tissue has already been resected.
CHEST TUBES
Left after lung resection to evacuate air and pleural fluid. Lecturer usually uses one chest tube, though two may sometimes be inserted depending on the case.

VATS

Notes

VATS — Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery

VariantDetail
Multi-port VATSTraditionally 3–4 ports.
Uniportal / single-portPerformed through one main incision. Rationale: fewer intercostal spaces violated, less intercostal nerve injury, potentially less pain and paresthesia. The camera may pass through the same operating incision, or occasionally use a separate camera port.
EVIDENCE NOTE
There are no definitive studies establishing superiority of multi-port versus single-port VATS; the approach depends heavily on surgeon training and preference.

RATS

Notes

Comparing the Three Approaches

ApproachFor the surgeonFor the patient
OpenErgonomically easier — direct hand movement and controlMore traumatic because of the large thoracotomy/laparotomy
Conventional VATS / laparoscopyCan be ergonomically more difficult — long instruments, restricted instrument movementBetter — minimally invasive
Robotic (RATS) introduced.Highly articulated instruments with greater range of motion, 3D visualization, and a seated console that improves ergonomics Current robotic systems commonly use multiple robotic arms; single-port robotic systems are also being developed andMinimally invasive — combines the advantages of both

Palliative care

  • Pain
  • Pleural effusion
  • Hemoptysis.
Notes

Palliation in Advanced Lung Cancer

REFRAME THIS
Palliative does not mean "do nothing." Patients with stage IV or advanced unresectable disease should receive active treatment of symptoms to improve quality of life.
SymptomDirected intervention
PainPain specialist / appropriate analgesic management
Pleural effusionDrainage
HemoptysisBronchoscopic / endobronchial intervention when appropriate to control bleeding
not curable.The goal is to make the patient's remaining life as comfortable and functional as possible, even when the cancer itself is
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 ≤3 cm = nodule; >3 cm = mass — and an SPN is by definition an incidental finding in an asymptomatic patient.
2 Screening = asymptomatic target population, no known abnormality. Surveillance = following a known abnormality.
Diagnosis = prompted by symptoms.
3 Screening criteria: age ≥50 plus ≥20 pack-years → annual LDCT; an abnormality moves the patient off annual
screening and onto a nodule algorithm.
4 NLST ~20% mortality reduction; major European trial ~30%. CXR screening failed.
5 Predictors of malignancy in an SPN: older age, smoking, prior cancer, increasing diameter, spiculated margins,
upper-lobe location.
6 Neuroendocrine spectrum: typical carcinoid = best prognosis, SCLC = worst — same cell of origin, very different
behavior.
7 SCLC is usually non-resectable because it presents late — but a small localized SCLC can still be operated on.
8 Tissue diagnosis before treatment; diagnosis before staging. Never treat on imaging alone.
9 Peripheral → CT-guided biopsy. Central → bronchoscopy.
10 Increased PET uptake ≠ cancer — infection and inflammation light up too. Brain metastasis → MRI, because
normal brain is hypermetabolic on PET.
11 N1 = ipsilateral hilar (still resect first; add adjuvant chemo). N2 = ipsilateral mediastinal (changes initial
management). N3 = contralateral (usually inoperable).
12 EBUS = less invasive; mediastinoscopy = higher tissue yield. Mediastinoscopy's feared complications are
azygos-vein injury and esophageal injury → mediastinitis.
13 Resectability = tumor/stage. Operability = patient/function (PFTs). Curative surgery needs both.
14 Cancer → anatomical resection (segmentectomy, lobectomy, pneumonectomy); wedge is non-anatomical and is for
diagnosis, benign disease and metastases. Lobectomy is the workhorse.
15 Use the least lung resection that achieves adequate oncologic treatment; converting to thoracotomy is right
whenever it serves complete resection or patient safety.
16 Palliative ≠ do nothing: pain → specialist analgesia, effusion → drainage, hemoptysis → bronchoscopic intervention.
